newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland awaits new, smaller flood swell on Odra.
newsitem.headline: Poland awaits new, smaller flood swell on Odra.

text.p: A new high-water swell advanced along Poland's Odra river on Wednesday but authorities said it was not likely to renew the full havoc of the last two weeks.

The floods, which have killed 55 people, continued to torment hundreds of thousands in the west and south while Warsaw authorities grappled with the economic and political fallout in the approach to September 21 general elections.

Flood crisis committee official Marek Sobczak said the latest Odra flood wave would reach the southwestern city of Opole late on Wednesday and would probably later inundate the residential estate of Zacisze in Wroclaw, further north.
But he said the swell, caused by heavy weekend rains, would be no repeat of the earlier calamity that drowned downtown Opole and much of Wroclaw in up to two metres of water.
"We should not expect another catastrophe on the same scale as early this month," Sobczak said.
He said there would also be new flooding along the Warta river, which had reversed its flow as it merged with the brimming Odra by Kostrzyn on the German border.
Other communities had already fallen victim to the latest rains, which heaped misery on a country staggering from the effects of downpours more than two weeks ago.
Many of the hundreds of thousands of people whose homes had already been damaged were still waiting for the waters to drain so they could begin to clean up and rebuild.
According to Sobczak 518 communities were still flooded, 12 of them totally, out of a total of 1,278 towns and villages that had been struck by the disaster.
Of the 5,972 sq km of Poland that had been swamped, 2,710 sq km were still under water, while 52,300 evacuees were still unable to return to their homes.
Weather forecasts for the next few days offered hope.
"In the coming two days we are expecting occasional showers over the area...but there will be no heavy, continual rains," a Meteorology and Water Management Institute official said.
But the receding waters left a nightmare scene. Some towns appeared to have been bombed, with smashed houses, derelict hospitals, broken bridges and roads like lunar landscapes.
Each hour brought appalling new statistics. Six weeks before the start of the school term, the education ministry reported damage to 601 schools and related establishments.
The opposition and the Peasant party, junior partner in Poland's ruling coalition, said elections should not go ahead on September 21 as traumatised areas needed longer to recover.
They urged the president to declare a state of emergency there, which might aid relief efforts and would automatically postpone polls until three months after it was lifted.

But President Aleksander Kwasniewski, backing his allies in the ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), said flood-hit areas would recover enough to hold the elections as planned, PAP news agency reported from Szczecin in the north.
The ex-communists say the polls should happen as scheduled to show that Poland's democracy was strong and stable.
On Tuesday the government adopted a three part programme to hasten flood relief, rebuild infrastracture and in the long term improve Poland's inadequate flood defence system.
It has also lined up funds by borrowing and reallocations from other projects in this year's budget to deal with the disaster which has caused billions of dollars of damage.
